entries.name: Biopharmaceutical phase and membrane passage (passive diffusion, Fick's law, carriers)
entries.memo: Only what is **dissolved** is absorbed: most drugs cross by **diffusion (Fick)**, hydrophilic ones need a **carrier**.

segments.label: Definition
segments.value: the **active ingredient** is the molecule that binds a **target** (receptor in the broad sense) and produces a therapeutic, prophylactic or diagnostic effect; the **dosage form** = active ingredient + inert **excipients**. Absorption is preceded by the **biopharmaceutical phase**: disintegration and **dissolution** → only drug **in solution** crosses membranes. «Dosis sola facit venenum»: every drug is also a potential poison → **risk/benefit** balance.

segments.label: How it works
segments.value: most drugs cross by **passive diffusion** down their gradient; hydrophilic or charged molecules use **carriers** (facilitated diffusion, secondary active transport): **levodopa**, α-methyldopa, baclofen → amino acid transporters; **β-lactams** → peptide transporter (PEPT1); **metformin** → organic cation transporters (OCT); macromolecules → endocytosis.

segments.label: Formula / key numbers
segments.value: **Fick's law: J = D · A · (C₁ − C₂) / thickness** → flux ↑ with gradient and **surface area**, ↓ with **thickness**; D summarizes size, **lipid solubility** (oil/water partition coefficient) and ionization. Blood carries the absorbed drug away (**sink effect**) → the gradient is maintained.

segments.label: Why it matters
segments.value: **surface area**: small intestine (villi, microvilli) ≫ stomach; intestinal disease ↓ absorption. **Thickness**: the same topical corticosteroid crosses the eyelid or an infant's skin far more than the heel. **Large molecules** (proteins, antibodies, heparin) do not diffuse → parenteral route.

segments.label: Exam trap
segments.value: **more lipophilic does not always mean better absorbed**: a partition coefficient that is too high «traps» the drug in the lipid bilayer and hinders its passage to cytosol and plasma; too low → it does not cross. A **hydrophilic–lipophilic balance** is needed.

segments.label: Connections
segments.value: → pKa and ion trapping (G1); P-glycoprotein (G1); levodopa and protein meals (B6); parenteral biologics (A9).

entries.name: pKa, Henderson–Hasselbalch equation and ion trapping
entries.nameShort: pKa, Henderson–Hasselbalch equation and ion trapping
entries.memo: Only the **non-ionized** form crosses: an acid gets **trapped** where the medium is basic, a base where it is acidic.

segments.label: Definition
segments.value: nearly all drugs are **weak acids or bases**; the **pKa** is the pH at which the drug is **50%** ionized. Only the **non-ionized** (lipid-soluble) form crosses membranes by diffusion; the charged form is hydrophilic and stays in its compartment.

segments.label: Formula / key numbers
segments.value: **weak acid**: log([HA]/[A⁻]) = pKa − pH → at pH < pKa HA (non-ionized) predominates. **Weak base**: log([BH⁺]/[B]) = pKa − pH → at pH < pKa BH⁺ (ionized) predominates. Each pH unit of difference = factor of **10**. Example: acid with pKa 4.4 → ionized/non-ionized ratio **1000:1 in plasma (pH 7.4)** and **1:1000 in gastric juice (pH 1.4)**.

segments.label: How it works
segments.value: **ion trapping**: at equilibrium an **acid accumulates in the more basic compartment**, a **base in the more acidic one**, because it ionizes there and cannot diffuse back. Applications: **urine** (alkalinizing with NaHCO₃ speeds excretion of salicylates and phenobarbital), **breast milk** and **fetal plasma** (more acidic than maternal plasma → concentrate weak bases).

segments.label: Clinical example
segments.value: **aspirin** (acid, pKa ≈ 3.5): non-ionized in the stomach → enters mucosal cells, where at pH ~7 it ionizes and is trapped (local contribution to gastric injury, besides COX-1 inhibition). **Morphine** (base): protonated at gastric pH → practically not absorbed in the stomach.

segments.label: Exam trap
segments.value: «is aspirin absorbed in the stomach because it is non-ionized there?» → absorption **starts** there, but **most** occurs in the **small intestine** (pH ~6.5): the huge surface area and blood flow outweigh the greater ionization. pH explains the **direction**, surface area decides the **amount**.

segments.label: Connections
segments.value: → renal excretion and urinary pH (G3); NSAIDs and gastric injury (A5); local anaesthetics, weak bases (B2).

entries.name: Routes of administration and first-pass effect
entries.nameShort: Routes of administration and first-pass effect
entries.memo: By mouth the drug passes **through the liver first**: **sublingual** avoids it, **rectal** only halfway.

segments.label: Definition
segments.value: **enteral routes** (oral, sublingual, rectal), **parenteral** (intravenous, intramuscular, subcutaneous, intra-arterial, intrathecal), **inhalational**, **topical/transdermal**; each can act **systemically** or **locally**. **First pass**: the fraction of an oral dose removed by the **gut wall** (CYP3A4, esterases, P-gp) and **liver** (portal route) **before** reaching the systemic circulation → ↓ bioavailability.

segments.label: How it works
segments.value: **oral**: convenient, cheap, safe (partly retrievable) but onset ~30–60 min and variable absorption. **Sublingual**: drains into the superior vena cava → **no first pass** (nitroglycerin). **Rectal**: about **50%** bypasses the liver → partial first pass; useful with vomiting or uncooperative patients. **IV**: 100% bioavailability, immediate effect, large volumes, but slow infusion and higher risk. **IM/SC**: absorption tunable by formulation (depots, long-acting insulins).

segments.label: Clinical example
segments.value: high first pass: **nitroglycerin** (ineffective orally → sublingual or patch), **propranolol**, **lidocaine**, **morphine**, verapamil, nifedipine, tricyclics. **Food** ↑ propranolol bioavailability (↑ splanchnic flow) → take it consistently with respect to meals. Luminal interactions: **tetracyclines + Ca²⁺/Mg²⁺/Al³⁺** (insoluble chelates), **penicillin G** destroyed by acid, **bile acid resins** + digoxin, **metoclopramide** advances and **anticholinergics** delay the peak (gastric emptying).

segments.label: Why it matters
segments.value: to stay **local**: **charged** drugs (tiotropium, quaternary ammonium), a **vasoconstrictor** with local anaesthetics, inhaled corticosteroids with high first pass (fluticasone, budesonide), particle size and spacers. But a topical route can become **systemic**: skin corticosteroids in children, **β-blocker eye drops** (bradycardia, bronchospasm).

segments.label: Exam trap
segments.value: «sublingual is fast because the surface is large» → **false**: the surface is small; it is fast because of **high vascularity**, **portal bypass** and use with **highly lipid-soluble**, non-ionized drugs (nitroglycerin).

segments.label: Connections
segments.value: → bioavailability (G1); P-glycoprotein (G1); CYP3A4 and grapefruit (G2); inhaled corticosteroids (A4, A8); nitrates (B12b).

entries.name: P-glycoprotein (P-gp, MDR1/ABCB1)
entries.memo: P-gp **pumps out** the intact drug: less absorption, more excretion, brain and fetus protected.

segments.label: Definition
segments.value: **ATP-dependent efflux pump** of the **ABC** family (gene **ABCB1/MDR1**) on the **luminal/apical** side of enterocytes, hepatocytes (bile canaliculus), proximal tubule, **blood–brain barrier endothelium**, placenta, testis. It extrudes amphipathic/lipophilic substrates **without modifying them**.

segments.label: How it works
segments.value: in the gut it **returns** part of the absorbed drug **to the lumen** (↓ bioavailability); in liver and kidney it **speeds excretion** (bile, urine); at the BBB and placenta it **protects** the CNS and fetus. It works in tandem with enterocyte **CYP3A4**, sharing many substrates and inhibitors → combined effect on oral bioavailability.

segments.label: Clinical example
segments.value: substrates: **digoxin**, quinidine, verapamil, diltiazem, **ciclosporin**, tacrolimus, **loperamide**, fexofenadine, HIV protease inhibitors, erythromycin, anticancer drugs (**doxorubicin, vincristine, etoposide**). Inhibitors (quinidine, verapamil, clarithromycin, ritonavir) → **↑ digoxin levels**; **PXR** inducers (**rifampicin, St John's wort**) → ↓ digoxin bioavailability.

segments.label: Why it matters
segments.value: **loperamide + quinidine**: P-gp inhibition at the BBB lets a normally peripheral opioid into the CNS → **respiratory depression**. In tumours, P-gp **overexpression** causes **multidrug resistance** (MDR) to structurally unrelated chemotherapeutics.

segments.label: Exam trap
segments.value: P-gp is **not an enzyme**: it does not metabolize, it **pumps out** the intact drug. A «P-gp interaction» changes exposure without new metabolites and often coexists with a CYP3A4 interaction.

segments.label: Connections
segments.value: → digoxin (B11b); antidiarrhoeals – loperamide (A11); clarithromycin (Antibiotici-3); chemotherapy resistance (B14); enzyme inducers (G2).

entries.name: Bioavailability (F) and the concentration–time curve (AUC, Cmax, Tmax)
entries.memo: F = how much drug **actually reaches** the circulation: **AUC** tells how much, **Cmax and Tmax** how fast.

segments.label: Definition
segments.value: **bioavailability (F)** = fraction of the dose reaching the systemic circulation **unchanged** (0–100%). **Absolute**: versus the intravenous route (F = 100% by definition); **relative**: between two formulations or two non-IV routes.

segments.label: Formula / key numbers
segments.value: **F = (AUC_oral × Dose_IV) / (AUC_IV × Dose_oral)**. **AUC** (area under the curve, e.g. trapezoidal method) = **extent** of exposure; **Cmax** and **Tmax** = **rate** of absorption. Example: oral digoxin **F ≈ 0.7** → the oral dose must be ~1.4 times the IV dose for the same exposure.

segments.label: How it works
segments.value: on the concentration–time curve: rising phase (absorption > distribution + elimination), **peak** (balance), falling phase (distribution, metabolism, excretion). **Onset** = time to exceed the **minimum effective concentration (MEC)**; **duration of action** ≈ time above the MEC; above the **minimum toxic concentration** adverse effects appear → the range between them is the **therapeutic window**.

segments.label: Why it matters
segments.value: oral F is reduced by acid and digestive enzymes, poor solubility, **P-gp**, intestinal and hepatic **first pass**, gastric emptying, gut disease. F is used to **convert doses between routes**: loading and maintenance doses are divided by F.

segments.label: Exam trap
segments.value: same AUC ≠ same effect: two formulations with equal F may have **different Cmax/Tmax** (one exceeds the MEC, the other does not or does so late). That is why **bioequivalence** requires AUC **and** Cmax.

segments.label: Connections
segments.value: → bioequivalence (G1); loading and maintenance doses (G3); first pass (G1).

entries.name: Bioequivalence: generic medicines vs biosimilars
entries.memo: A generic must give the **same exposure** (90% CI within **80–125%**); a biosimilar must also show **efficacy and safety**.

segments.label: Definition
segments.value: two **pharmaceutically equivalent** products (same active ingredient, strength, dosage form and route) are **bioequivalent** if the **rate and extent** of absorption (AUC, Cmax, Tmax) do not differ significantly. This underpins approval of **generics** when the patent expires: excipients may change, exposure may not.

segments.label: Formula / key numbers
segments.value: **EMA/FDA criterion**: the **90% confidence interval** of the test/reference ratio (geometric means) of **AUC and Cmax** must lie within **80.00–125.00%** (symmetric on a log scale). For **narrow-therapeutic-index** drugs the EMA narrows it to **90.00–111.11%** (at least for AUC).

segments.label: Why it matters
segments.value: a generic **omits** preclinical and clinical efficacy studies: the bioequivalence study «transfers» the originator's data. A **biosimilar** cannot: a protein made by living cells is never identical («the process makes the product») → a **comparability exercise** on quality, non-clinical and **clinical** data (efficacy, safety, **immunogenicity**) is required.

segments.label: Exam trap
segments.value: «80–125% means a generic may contain 20% less drug» → **false**: the limit applies to the **confidence interval of the exposure ratio**, not to drug content (which has much tighter quality limits); observed mean differences are a few percent. But each generic is compared with the **reference**, not with other generics.

segments.label: Connections
segments.value: → biosimilars (A9); bioavailability (G1); therapeutic index (G4).

entries.name: Plasma protein binding (albumin, α1-acid glycoprotein) and displacement
entries.memo: Only the **free fraction** acts, is filtered and metabolized; displacement raises it only **transiently**.

segments.label: Definition
segments.value: in plasma a drug is in **dynamic equilibrium** between **free** and **bound** forms (weak, reversible bonds). Only the **free fraction** crosses membranes, reaches the target, is **filtered** by the glomerulus and (for low-extraction drugs) **metabolized**; the bound fraction is a **reservoir** that prolongs its stay. % bound = bound/total × 100.

segments.label: How it works
segments.value: **albumin** → **acidic** drugs (site I: **warfarin**, NSAIDs, sulfonylureas, valproate, furosemide; site II: **diazepam**, ibuprofen); **α1-acid glycoprotein** (an **acute-phase** protein) → **basic** drugs (**lidocaine**); **lipoproteins** → highly lipophilic drugs (amiodarone); specific carrier proteins (transcortin, SHBG, TBG) → steroids and hormones.

segments.label: Formula / key numbers
segments.value: **very high** binding (≥95–99%): **warfarin ~99%**, **ibuprofen >99%**, amiodarone, valproate (~90%, saturable at high doses); **low**: **metformin**, **paracetamol**, allopurinol. When sites **saturate**, the free fraction rises more than proportionally with dose.

segments.label: Why it matters
segments.value: the free fraction ↑ with **hypoalbuminaemia** (liver disease, nephrotic syndrome, malnutrition, burns, pregnancy); in **acute-phase reactions** (MI, cancer, arthritis, Crohn's) ↑ α1-acid glycoprotein → ↑ binding of bases. Plasma assays usually measure the **total**: with low albumin a «normal» level can hide too much free drug.

segments.label: Exam trap
segments.value: **displacement** (e.g. NSAIDs competing with warfarin at site I): the rise in free fraction is **transient** — the released drug distributes and is eliminated, and at **steady state the free concentration returns to baseline unless clearance changes**. It matters mainly for **narrow-therapeutic-index, high-clearance, IV** drugs (e.g. lidocaine). The warfarin + NSAID risk is mostly **pharmacodynamic** (antiplatelet effect, gastric lesions) and, for some NSAIDs, **CYP2C9** inhibition.

segments.label: Connections
segments.value: → oral anticoagulants (B12); volume of distribution (G2); clearance (G3).

entries.name: Tissue distribution: perfusion, blood–brain barrier, tissue affinity and redistribution
entries.nameShort: Tissue distribution: perfusion, blood–brain barrier, tissue affinity and redistribution
entries.memo: Drug goes **first where blood flow is highest**, then where it finds **affinity**: waking from thiopental is **redistribution**.

segments.label: Definition
segments.value: passage of drug **from plasma to tissues** (interstitium → cells). It depends on **free fraction**, organ **perfusion**, **capillary/barrier type**, physicochemical **affinity** for the tissue (lipid solubility, specific binding) and **transporters**. Drug also reaches tissues without the target → **depots** and adverse effects.

segments.label: Formula / key numbers
segments.value: resting blood flow (70 kg): **kidney ~20%** of cardiac output (highest per gram), **liver ~31%**, **brain ~15%**, heart ~4.5%; **muscle** ~16% but little per kg; **fat** ~4.5% and very slow → highly perfused organs equilibrate first, fat last.

segments.label: How it works
segments.value: **fenestrated** capillaries (liver, kidney, spleen, gut, endocrine glands) even let antibodies through; the **BBB** (tight junctions + P-gp) admits only **small, lipophilic, non-ionized** molecules or those with a transporter: **dopamine** does not cross → **levodopa** is given; **tubocurarine** (quaternary ammonium) stays peripheral.

segments.label: Clinical example
segments.value: **thiopental**: after an IV bolus it reaches the brain at once; awakening depends on **redistribution** to muscle and fat, not on metabolism. **Lidocaine in shock**: hypoperfused muscle → more drug to the CNS → **seizures**. **Azithromycin**: intracellular/tissue levels (including phagocytes) far above plasma → short courses. **Bisphosphonates** → bone (pyrophosphate analogues); **tetracyclines** → bones and teeth (chelate Ca²⁺).

segments.label: Exam trap
segments.value: «should a drug that accumulates in fat be given by another route?» → **no**: distribution happens **after** entry into the circulation and depends on the molecule, not the route; the route changes bioavailability and absorption rate. Fat storage matters in **chronic therapy** (lipophilic benzodiazepines: slow, unpredictable release, more so in the elderly with more fat mass).

segments.label: Connections
segments.value: → intravenous anaesthetics (B2); benzodiazepines (B1); azithromycin (Antibiotici-3); bisphosphonates (A12); levodopa (B6).

entries.name: Apparent volume of distribution (Vd)
entries.memo: Vd is an **imaginary** volume: small if the drug stays in the blood, **huge** if it hides in tissues.

segments.label: Definition
segments.value: **Vd = amount of drug in the body / plasma concentration** (after an IV bolus: Dose/C₀). It is the **theoretical** volume needed to hold all the drug at the concentration measured in plasma: a **distribution** parameter, not an anatomical space.

segments.label: Formula / key numbers
segments.value: references (70 kg): **plasma ~3–4 L (~0.05 L/kg)**, **extracellular fluid ~14 L (~0.2 L/kg)**, **total body water ~42 L (~0.6 L/kg)**. Examples: **heparin ~0.05–0.1 L/kg** (stays in plasma), **warfarin ~0.1–0.2** (albumin-bound), tubocurarine ~0.2 (extracellular), theophylline ~0.5, **digoxin ~6 L/kg (~500 L)**, **chloroquine ~15,000 L**.

segments.label: How it works
segments.value: **small** Vd: hydrophilic, large or highly plasma-protein-bound drug → stays in the vascular compartment. **Large** Vd (above total body water): drug **sequestered in tissues** (lipids, tissue proteins and phospholipids) → low plasma concentration.

segments.label: Why it matters
segments.value: **loading dose = target C × Vd / F**: theophylline, Vd 0.5 L/kg × 70 kg = 35 L, target 10 mg/L → **350 mg**. **t½ = 0.693 × Vd / CL** → at equal clearance a large Vd prolongs t½ (amiodarone: weeks). Small Vd → **haemodialysis works** in poisoning; large Vd (tricyclics, digoxin) → dialysis is useless.

segments.label: Exam trap
segments.value: a Vd of 15,000 L is not a calculation error: it says almost all the drug is **in tissues**, but **not where**. Vd changes with age, obesity, oedema: diazepam has a longer t½ in the elderly because of **↑ Vd**, not ↓ clearance.

segments.label: Connections
segments.value: → protein binding (G2); half-life and loading dose (G3); digoxin (B11b).

entries.name: Biotransformation: phase 1 (CYP450) and phase 2 (conjugation) reactions
entries.memo: **Phase 1** adds a polar handle (often via **CYP**), **phase 2** attaches a conjugate: the result is an **excretable** drug.

segments.label: Definition
segments.value: set of reactions (mainly **hepatic**, also intestinal, renal, pulmonary) that make a drug **more polar** → excretable in urine or bile; usually they end its activity. **Phase 1 (functionalization)**: introduces or unmasks a polar group (–OH, –COOH, –NH₂, –SH). **Phase 2 (conjugation)**: attaches a highly polar endogenous substrate.

segments.label: How it works
segments.value: **phase 1**: **oxidations** (CYP450 = **haem** monooxygenases: Fe³⁺, reduced by electrons from NADPH, binds O₂ and inserts one oxygen atom into the substrate: RH + O₂ + NADPH + H⁺ → ROH + H₂O + NADP⁺), reductions, **hydrolysis** (esterases: aspirin → salicylate; enalapril → enalaprilat). **Phase 2**: **glucuronidation** (UGT, the most important), sulfation (SULT), **acetylation** (NAT2), **glutathione** conjugation (GST), **methylation** (COMT, TPMT).

segments.label: Formula / key numbers
segments.value: nomenclature: **CYP + family (number) + subfamily (letter) + isoform (number)** → CYP**3A4**. A few isoforms of families 1–3 metabolize most drugs; **CYP3A4**, the most abundant in liver, is involved in **over 50%** of drugs in use.

segments.label: Clinical example
segments.value: **phenytoin** → 4-hydroxyphenytoin (CYP) → glucuronide (UGT): from an almost insoluble molecule to a water-soluble metabolite. **Statins**: lova-, simva-, atorvastatin → **CYP3A4**; fluvastatin → **CYP2C9**; **pravastatin** (and rosuvastatin) little CYP-dependent → preferred with 3A4 inhibitors (macrolides, azoles) to reduce **myopathy/rhabdomyolysis** risk.

segments.label: Exam trap
segments.value: phase 2 does **not always follow** phase 1 (oxazepam and lorazepam are glucuronidated directly) and does not always increase water solubility: **acetylation and methylation** can reduce it. **Neonates** have immature UGTs (physiological jaundice; chloramphenicol «grey baby» syndrome).

segments.label: Connections
segments.value: → inducers and inhibitors (G2); active metabolites and prodrugs (G2); polymorphisms (G2); statins (B9).

entries.name: CYP inducers and inhibitors (and grapefruit juice)
entries.memo: **Inhibitors** raise levels within **hours**; **inducers** lower them over **days** and wear off slowly.

segments.label: Definition
segments.value: **induction** = ↑ **synthesis** of enzymes (and transporters such as P-gp) via nuclear receptors (**PXR**: rifampicin, St John's wort; **CAR**: phenobarbital; **AhR**: smoking, omeprazole) → ↑ clearance → **↓ concentrations and effect**. **Inhibition** = competitive or irreversible («suicide») block → ↓ clearance → **↑ concentrations and toxicity**.

segments.label: Formula / key numbers
segments.value: **timing**: inhibition appears within **hours–a few days** (depends on the inhibitor's t½); induction needs **days–1/2 weeks** (protein synthesis) and **persists** for days after withdrawal (enzyme turnover).

segments.label: Clinical example
segments.value: **inducers**: **rifampicin** (the strongest), **carbamazepine** (also autoinduction), **phenytoin**, **phenobarbital**, **St John's wort**, cigarette smoke (CYP1A2), chronic ethanol (CYP2E1). **Inhibitors**: **erythromycin/clarithromycin** (not azithromycin), **azoles** (ketoconazole, itraconazole, voriconazole), **ritonavir**, cimetidine, amiodarone, **valproate**, SSRIs (**fluoxetine/paroxetine → CYP2D6**; fluvoxamine → 1A2/2C19), **grapefruit juice** (furanocoumarins → CYP3A4).

segments.label: Why it matters
segments.value: **rifampicin + oral contraceptive** → contraceptive failure; **clarithromycin + simvastatin** → rhabdomyolysis; **terfenadine + erythromycin/grapefruit** → long QT and torsades (terfenadine withdrawn); ketoconazole + protease inhibitors → toxicity. Harm is greater when the victim drug has a **narrow therapeutic index**.

segments.label: Exam trap
segments.value: **grapefruit** inhibits mainly **intestinal** CYP3A4 **irreversibly** → raises the **oral** bioavailability of high-first-pass substrates (felodipine, simvastatin, ciclosporin, midazolam), not the clearance of an IV drug; the effect lasts **1–3 days** (new enzyme must be synthesized) → spacing doses by a few hours is not enough.

segments.label: Connections
segments.value: → rifampicin (Antibiotici-2); macrolides (Antibiotici-3); statins (B9); carbamazepine (B4); SSRIs (B3).

entries.name: Active metabolites, reactive intermediates and prodrugs (benzodiazepines, paracetamol, clopidogrel, codeine)
entries.nameShort: Active metabolites, reactive intermediates and prodrugs
entries.memo: Metabolism can **prolong** the effect (nordiazepam), make it **toxic** (NAPQI) or **switch it on** (prodrugs).

segments.label: Definition
segments.value: metabolism does not always inactivate: it can produce **active metabolites** (prolonging the effect), **reactive intermediates** (covalent binding to proteins and DNA → toxicity, typically hepatic) or activate a **prodrug** (given inactive, activated by metabolism).

segments.label: Clinical example
segments.value: **active metabolites**: **diazepam → nordiazepam → oxazepam** (all active; nordiazepam has a very long half-life → overall effect lasting days) → inactive glucuronide. By contrast **oxazepam, lorazepam, temazepam** are only **glucuronidated** (inactive metabolites) → preferred in **elderly and liver patients**; triazolam, midazolam, alprazolam → CYP3A4, short duration.

segments.label: How it works
segments.value: **paracetamol**: mostly **glucuronidated and sulfated**; a small fraction → **CYP2E1** (and 3A4) → **NAPQI**, neutralized by **glutathione**. In **overdose** conjugation saturates, GSH is depleted and NAPQI binds proteins covalently → **centrilobular hepatic necrosis**. Antidote: **N-acetylcysteine** (restores GSH), most effective within **8–10 h**.

segments.label: Prodrugs
segments.value: **enalapril → enalaprilat** (esterases); **clopidogrel** → active metabolite in 2 steps via **CYP2C19** (only ~15% of the dose); **codeine → morphine** via **CYP2D6** (~5–10%); **levodopa → dopamine**; valaciclovir → aciclovir.

segments.label: Exam trap
segments.value: paracetamol toxicity ↑ when **GSH is low** or **CYP2E1 is induced**: chronic alcoholism, fasting or malnutrition, liver disease. And a prodrug activated by a **single polymorphic enzyme** (clopidogrel, codeine) is the textbook case for **pharmacogenetics**.

segments.label: Connections
segments.value: → paracetamol (A5); benzodiazepines (B1); P2Y12 antagonists (B12); weak opioids (B8); polymorphisms (G2).

entries.name: CYP polymorphisms and pharmacogenetics (CYP2C9, CYP2C19, CYP2D6, NAT2)
entries.memo: Same dose, opposite response: for a **prodrug** ultrarapid metabolizers risk **toxicity**, poor metabolizers **failure**.

segments.label: Definition
segments.value: **polymorphism** = gene variant present in **>1%** of the population. Metabolic phenotypes: **poor (PM)**, **intermediate (IM)**, **normal/extensive (EM)**, **ultrarapid (UM**, gene duplications). **Pharmacogenetics** studies how such variants change drug efficacy and toxicity.

segments.label: Formula / key numbers
segments.value: data reported in the lecture (≈360 healthy Italian volunteers): **CYP2C9** (*2/*3 variants) heterozygotes ~**32%**, two variant alleles ~**6%**; **CYP2C19** (*2) heterozygotes ~**19%**, homozygotes ~**1.7%**; **CYP2D6**: EM ~**53%**, heterozygotes ~**35%**, PM ~**3.4%**, **UM ~8.3%** (UMs more frequent in the **Mediterranean** area).

segments.label: Clinical example
segments.value: slow **CYP2C9** → **warfarin** degraded less → bleeding (lower doses, close INR). **CYP2C19** PM → **clopidogrel** not activated → **stent thrombosis** (prefer prasugrel or ticagrelor); but omeprazole more effective. **CYP2D6**: PM → **codeine ineffective** and nortriptyline accumulation; UM → excess morphine from codeine → **respiratory depression** (paediatric deaths: codeine contraindicated **under 12 years**). Slow **NAT2** acetylators → **isoniazid** toxicity.

segments.label: Why it matters
segments.value: it justifies **pre-prescription tests** (CYP2C19 for clopidogrel, CYP2C9/VKORC1 for warfarin, HLA-B for abacavir) and explains why the same dose gives opposite responses in different patients.

segments.label: Exam trap
segments.value: UM is **not always «better»**: for a **prodrug** (codeine) UM = **toxicity** and PM = failure; for an **active drug inactivated** by the CYP (nortriptyline) it is the reverse, PM = toxicity and UM = failure.

segments.label: Connections
segments.value: → P2Y12 antagonists and oral anticoagulants (B12); weak opioids (B8); PPIs (A11); isoniazid (Antibiotici-2).

entries.name: Elimination routes and enterohepatic circulation
entries.memo: A glucuronide excreted in bile can be **reabsorbed** after bacterial hydrolysis: the drug **comes back** and lasts longer.

segments.label: Definition
segments.value: **main** routes: **kidney** (urine; hydrophilic molecules or those made so by metabolism) and **liver → bile → faeces**. **Minor** routes: **lungs** (volatile anaesthetics, ethanol → breathalyser), **sweat and saliva** (drug tests), **breast milk** (risk to the infant), **hair** (keratin; growth ~1 cm/month → dating exposure in forensic medicine).

segments.label: How it works
segments.value: **enterohepatic circulation**: conjugates (mainly **glucuronides**) excreted in bile are hydrolysed by **bacterial β-glucuronidases** → the free, again lipophilic drug is **reabsorbed** and returns to the liver. Consequences: ↑ residence time, **secondary peaks**, longer apparent half-life.

segments.label: Clinical example
segments.value: **indomethacin**: steady-state t½ ~2.4 h but **terminal t½ ~120 h**, attributed to biliary cycling. Lecture example: **digoxin** may show rebounds in concentration hours later; **digitoxin** (more lipophilic, mainly hepatic elimination, marked enterohepatic cycling, half-life of days) was even harder to manage and has been abandoned.

segments.label: Why it matters
segments.value: the cycle can be **interrupted** by agents that bind metabolites in the gut (**bile acid sequestrants** such as cholestyramine, activated charcoal) → useful in poisoning, but a source of interactions (↓ absorption of digoxin, warfarin).

segments.label: Exam trap
segments.value: «antibiotics + the pill = pregnancy by blocking enterohepatic cycling» → weak evidence for common antibiotics; the **proven** interaction is **enzyme induction** (**rifampicin**). In **milk**, more acidic than plasma, **weak bases** concentrate.

segments.label: Connections
segments.value: → digoxin (B11b); resins and other lipid-lowering drugs (B9); rifampicin (Antibiotici-2); ion trapping (G1).

entries.name: Renal excretion: filtration, tubular secretion (OAT/OCT), reabsorption and urinary pH
entries.memo: The kidney **filters** free drug, **secretes** even bound drug via OAT/OCT, **reabsorbs** the non-ionized form: urinary pH decides the last step.

segments.label: Definition
segments.value: three processes: **glomerular filtration** (passive; only **free**, small drug: albumin does not pass), **active tubular secretion** (**proximal** tubule, transporters; the main determinant of renal excretion), **passive reabsorption** (mainly distal; depends on lipid solubility, pKa and **urinary pH**).

segments.label: How it works
segments.value: **OAT1/OAT3** (organic anions: **penicillins**, **NSAIDs**, **methotrexate**, diuretics, **probenecid**, urate) and **OCT2/MATE** (cations: **metformin**, cimetidine, trimethoprim, procainamide); P-gp for **digoxin**. Secretion is **not limited by protein binding**. **Morphine** (a base, via OCT) becomes an anion after glucuronidation → also via OAT.

segments.label: Clinical example
segments.value: **probenecid** competes with **penicillin** for OAT1/OAT3 → slows its excretion and prolongs its levels (historical strategy). **NSAIDs or probenecid + methotrexate** → ↓ excretion → toxicity. Uric acid: **furosemide/thiazides** ↑ uricaemia (gout); low-dose **aspirin** retains urate, high doses (>3 g/day) are uricosuric; probenecid also inhibits **URAT1** (uricosuric).

segments.label: Urinary pH and special populations
segments.value: **urinary ion trapping**: **weak acid → alkalinize** urine (**NaHCO₃**: salicylates, phenobarbital) → A⁻ trapped; **weak base → acidify** (NH₄Cl; amphetamines) → BH⁺ trapped, now rarely used (acidosis, rhabdomyolysis). **Neonates**: immature secretion; **elderly**: progressively ↓ renal function → dose by **eGFR** (Cockcroft–Gault, CKD-EPI).

segments.label: Exam trap
segments.value: «a highly protein-bound drug cannot be eliminated by the kidney» → true for **filtration**, not for **active secretion**, which strips drug even from proteins (penicillins are cleared rapidly despite binding).

segments.label: Connections
segments.value: → β-lactams; diuretics (B11b); metformin (A10); NSAIDs (A5); ion trapping (G1).

entries.name: First-order and zero-order (saturable) elimination kinetics
entries.memo: First order = a fixed **percentage** is lost; zero order = a fixed **amount**: with **phenytoin** small dose increases do big harm.

segments.label: Definition
segments.value: **first order**: elimination rate is **proportional to concentration** → a **constant fraction** is removed per unit time; **exponential** decline (straight line on a semi-log plot), **constant t½**. **Zero order**: the system is **saturated** → a **constant amount** is removed per unit time; **linear** decline, t½ not constant.

segments.label: Formula / key numbers
segments.value: **C(t) = C₀ · e^(−k·t)**, with **k = CL/Vd = 0.693/t½**. Michaelis–Menten: **v = Vmax · C / (Km + C)** → when C ≪ Km kinetics are first order; when C ≫ Km they become zero order. After 3 t½ 12.5% remains, after 5 t½ about 3%.

segments.label: Clinical example
segments.value: **ethanol**: alcohol dehydrogenase saturated even at low concentrations → roughly constant elimination (about **7–10 g/h**). **Phenytoin**: Km (5–10 mg/L) close to the lower end of the therapeutic range (10–20 mg/L) → small dose increases give **large rises** in concentration. High-dose **salicylates**.

segments.label: Why it matters
segments.value: with saturable elimination the steady-state concentration is **not proportional to dose**, steady state comes later and unpredictably and a constant t½ no longer applies → **therapeutic drug monitoring (TDM)** and small, gradual dose increases.

segments.label: Exam trap
segments.value: the lecture also lists other antiepileptics as saturable; the paradigm case to bring is **phenytoin**. **Carbamazepine** is famous for something else: **autoinduction** (clearance ↑ over the first weeks → the dose must be raised).

segments.label: Connections
segments.value: → antiepileptics (B9); aspirin (A5); clearance and half-life (G3).

entries.name: Clearance (CL): renal, hepatic and total
entries.memo: Clearance sets the **maintenance dose**: dosing rate = **CL × desired concentration**.

segments.label: Definition
segments.value: **volume of plasma (or blood) completely cleared of drug per unit time** (mL/min, L/h): **CL = elimination rate / concentration**. It is **additive**: total CL = renal CL + hepatic CL + other.

segments.label: Formula / key numbers
segments.value: at **steady state**: dosing rate = **CL × Css** → **maintenance dose = Css × CL × τ / F**. Lecture example: **clonidine**, CL 3 mL/min/kg, target 1 ng/mL → infusion **3 ng/min/kg** (~0.2 µg/min in 70 kg). Hepatic: **CL_H = Q_H × E** (Q_H ~0.8–1.5 L/min; E = extraction ratio).

segments.label: How it works
segments.value: **high-extraction** drugs (E → 1; systemic CL > ~6 mL/min/kg: **lidocaine, propranolol, morphine, diltiazem, imipramine**) → CL limited by **hepatic blood flow** (↓ in heart failure, shock) and large first pass. **Low extraction** (e.g. warfarin, phenytoin, theophylline) → CL depends on **free fraction** and **enzyme activity** (inducers, inhibitors).

segments.label: Why it matters
segments.value: it is the key parameter for **chronic therapy**: it sets the **maintenance dose**. If CL ↓ (renal failure for aminoglycosides, digoxin, metformin; hepatic failure for metabolized drugs) and the dose is unchanged → **accumulation** and toxicity.

segments.label: Exam trap
segments.value: CL is a **proportionality constant**, not the amount eliminated (which also depends on concentration); and **t½ does not measure CL**: a drug can have high CL and a long t½ if its **Vd is huge**.

segments.label: Connections
segments.value: → half-life and dosing (G3); first pass (G1); renal excretion (G3); metabolism (G2).

entries.name: Half-life, steady state, loading dose and maintenance dose
entries.nameShort: Half-life, steady state, loading dose and maintenance dose
entries.memo: Steady state arrives in **4–5 half-lives** whatever the dose; if you cannot wait, use a **loading dose** (Vd).

segments.label: Definition
segments.value: **half-life (t½)** = time for the plasma concentration to **halve** (first-order kinetics). **Steady state** = the condition in which, with repeated doses or a constant infusion, **input rate = elimination rate** and concentrations fluctuate around a plateau.

segments.label: Formula / key numbers
segments.value: **t½ = 0.693 × Vd / CL**. Accumulation towards steady state: 1 t½ → 50%, 2 → 75%, 3 → 87.5%, **4 → ~94%**, **5 → ~97%** → the **4–5 half-life** rule (also for **washout**). **Loading dose = target C × Vd / F**; **maintenance dose = target C × CL × τ / F**. With dosing interval τ = t½ the concentration fluctuates two-fold.

segments.label: How it works
segments.value: the **time** to steady state depends **only on t½**; the **level** reached depends on dose, interval, F and CL. t½ «summarizes» distribution (Vd) and elimination (CL).

segments.label: Clinical example
segments.value: **lidocaine** (t½ 1–2 h) for a post-infarction arrhythmia: waiting 4 t½ (4–8 h) is unacceptable → **loading bolus + infusion**. **Digoxin** (t½ ~3 days): without loading it takes almost **2 weeks** → divided loading (e.g. 0.25 + 0.25 + 0.125 mg 6–8 h apart) with monitoring. Fluoxetine/norfluoxetine: steady state and washout over **weeks**.

segments.label: Exam trap
segments.value: **doubling the dose does not reach steady state sooner**: it doubles the level, not the time. The loading dose depends on **Vd**, the maintenance dose on **CL**: in renal failure mainly the maintenance dose is cut (but for digoxin Vd also falls → the loading dose must be reduced too).

segments.label: Connections
segments.value: → volume of distribution (G2); clearance (G3); digoxin (B11b); class I antiarrhythmics – lidocaine (B13).

entries.name: Drug–target interaction and the concentration–response curve: EC50, potency and efficacy
entries.nameShort: Drug–target interaction and the concentration–response curve: EC50, potency and efficacy
entries.memo: **Potency** = where the curve sits (EC50, x-axis); **efficacy** = how high it goes (Emax, y-axis).

segments.label: Definition
segments.value: **pharmacodynamics** studies what the drug does to the body. Targets: **receptors**, **ion channels**, **enzymes**, **transporters/pumps**. Binding is usually **weak and reversible** (H-bonds, ionic, van der Waals) → the effect ends when the drug dissociates; if **covalent** (aspirin–COX, PPIs–proton pump, clopidogrel–P2Y12) it lasts until the target is **resynthesized**.

segments.label: Formula / key numbers
segments.value: **response vs log[concentration]** curve = **sigmoid** with threshold, slope and **plateau (Emax)**. **EC50** (ED50 in vivo) = concentration or dose giving **50% of the maximal effect**. The log scale linearizes the central part and lets the EC50 be read accurately over a wide dose range.

segments.label: How it works
segments.value: **potency** = amount of drug needed for a given effect → **position on the x-axis** (lower EC50 = more potent; depends on affinity and coupling). **Efficacy** = **maximal attainable effect** → **height of the plateau**. A **steep slope** means small dose changes cause large effect changes → a less forgiving drug.

segments.label: Clinical example
segments.value: **furosemide vs hydrochlorothiazide**: furosemide (loop, NKCC2, where ~**25%** of filtered Na⁺ is reabsorbed) is **more efficacious** but **less potent** (20–40 mg needed); hydrochlorothiazide (distal tubule, NCC, maximal effect around 5% of filtered Na⁺) is **more potent** (12.5–25 mg) but **less efficacious**.

segments.label: Exam trap
segments.value: «more potent = better» → **false**: potency only decides **how many milligrams** are needed; what matters is **efficacy** relative to the goal. In **acute pulmonary oedema** furosemide is needed, because no thiazide dose reaches that plateau.

segments.label: Connections
segments.value: → diuretics (B11b); therapeutic index (G4); partial agonists (G4); antagonism (G4).

entries.name: Therapeutic index, therapeutic window and margin of safety
entries.nameShort: Therapeutic index, therapeutic window and margin of safety
entries.memo: **TI = TD50/ED50**: the narrower it is, the more every small change in exposure becomes **toxicity** → monitoring.

segments.label: Definition
segments.value: **quantal dose–response curves** (% of individuals responding) give the **ED50** (desired effect in 50%), **TD50** (toxicity in 50%) and, in animals, **LD50**. **Therapeutic index (TI) = TD50/ED50** (or LD50/ED50): it measures how **selective** a drug is for the desired versus the harmful effect.

segments.label: Formula / key numbers
segments.value: **therapeutic window** = concentration range effective with minimal toxicity. **Margin of safety** (lecture) = distance between the dose toxic in **1%** and the dose effective in **99%** (TD1/ED99): more conservative than the TI. G&G example: LD50 400 / ED50 100 → **TI = 4**.

segments.label: Clinical example
segments.value: **narrow therapeutic index**: **digoxin** (efficacy at concentrations ≤1 ng/mL), **lithium**, **warfarin**, **phenytoin**, **aminoglycosides**, theophylline, ciclosporin/tacrolimus → **monitoring** (plasma levels, INR). Lecture: for **barbiturates** the hypnotic dose is close to the lethal one, unlike benzodiazepines.

segments.label: Why it matters
segments.value: with a wide TI the drug «absorbs» pharmacokinetic variability (interactions, polymorphisms, organ failure); with a narrow TI small changes in **clearance** lead to toxicity → caution with inhibitors and inducers and tighter bioequivalence criteria.

segments.label: Exam trap
segments.value: the TI uses **50%** values: if efficacy and toxicity curves have **different slopes**, their tails may overlap even with an apparently good TI → hence the **margin of safety**. And the TI depends on which toxic effect is considered.

segments.label: Connections
segments.value: → digoxin (B11b); lithium (B4); warfarin (B12); aminoglycosides (Antibiotici-3); bioequivalence (G1).

entries.name: Full, partial and inverse agonists; antagonists (the opioid model)
entries.nameShort: Full, partial and inverse agonists; antagonists
entries.memo: All of them **bind** (affinity); what changes is how much they **activate**: full 100%, partial «ceiling», antagonist 0, inverse **below zero**.

segments.label: Definition
segments.value: **affinity** = ability to bind the receptor; **efficacy (intrinsic activity)** = ability to activate it. **Full agonist**: maximal response; **partial agonist**: occupies all receptors but gives a **sub-maximal** response («ceiling effect»); **neutral antagonist**: **zero** efficacy, seen only in the presence of an agonist; **inverse agonist**: **reduces constitutive activity** by stabilizing the inactive conformation.

segments.label: How it works
segments.value: **two-state** model (inactive R ⇄ active R*): an agonist shifts the equilibrium towards R*, a partial agonist only partly, an inverse agonist towards R, a neutral antagonist not at all. A **partial** agonist in the presence of a **full** one occupies the receptors and **reduces** its effect → it behaves as an **antagonist**.

segments.label: Clinical example
segments.value: **μ** receptor: **morphine** (full agonist: analgesia but also **respiratory depression**), **buprenorphine** (high-**affinity** partial agonist: ceiling on respiratory depression → safer; may precipitate withdrawal in full-agonist users), **naloxone** (competitive antagonist; short t½ → risk of **re-sedation**). Other partial agonists: **varenicline** (α4β2), buspirone (5-HT1A), aripiprazole (D2), **pindolol** (β, intrinsic sympathomimetic activity). Inverse agonists: **H1/H2 antihistamines**.

segments.label: Exam trap
segments.value: **partial ≠ weakly potent**: potency and efficacy are independent (buprenorphine is **more potent** than morphine but **less efficacious**). And an inverse agonist differs from an antagonist only where the receptor has **constitutive activity**.

segments.label: Connections
segments.value: → opioids (B8); antihistamines (A6); buspirone (B1); aripiprazole (B5); bupropion and varenicline (B3).

entries.name: Allosteric modulators: benzodiazepines and the GABA-A receptor
entries.nameShort: Allosteric modulators: benzodiazepines and the GABA-A receptor
entries.memo: Benzodiazepines **do not open** the channel by themselves: they make GABA **more effective** (more openings). No GABA, no effect.

segments.label: Definition
segments.value: **allosteric modulator** = ligand that binds a **site different** from that of the endogenous (**orthosteric**) ligand and changes its **affinity and/or efficacy**: positive (**PAM**), negative (**NAM**) or «silent» (occupies the site without effect, blocking other modulators).

segments.label: How it works
segments.value: **GABA-A**: pentamer (typically 2α, 2β, 1γ) forming a **Cl⁻** channel. **GABA** binds between **α and β**; **benzodiazepines** at the **α–γ** interface → ↑ affinity for GABA and ↑ **frequency** of channel opening **in the presence of GABA**. **Barbiturates** ↑ the **duration** of openings and at high doses open the channel **even without GABA**.

segments.label: Clinical example
segments.value: **flumazenil**: competitive antagonist at the BZ site (blocks both benzodiazepines and inverse agonists at that site) → overdose antidote and reversal of midazolam sedation. **Picrotoxin**: blocks the **pore** (non-competitive); **bicuculline**: competitive antagonist at the GABA site (convulsant, experimental only); **neurosteroids**: allopregnanolone PAM, pregnenolone sulfate NAM.

segments.label: Why it matters
segments.value: benzodiazepines amplify a **physiological** signal → «ceiling» effect → overdose of a benzodiazepine alone is rarely lethal; with **alcohol, barbiturates, opioids** the risk becomes serious. α subunits steer the effect (α1 sedation/amnesia; α2/α3 anxiolysis and muscle relaxation).

segments.label: Exam trap
segments.value: «benzodiazepines are GABA agonists» → **no**: without GABA they do not open the channel. **Flumazenil** has a shorter half-life than many benzodiazepines (**re-sedation**) and can trigger **seizures** in benzodiazepine-dependent patients or mixed overdoses (e.g. with tricyclics).

segments.label: Connections
segments.value: → benzodiazepines, flumazenil, barbiturates, neurosteroids (B1); ligand-gated channel superfamily (G6); synergism (G4).

entries.name: Antagonism: competitive, irreversible/non-competitive, functional and chemical
entries.nameShort: Antagonism: competitive, irreversible/non-competitive, functional and chemical
entries.memo: **Competitive** = curve shifted right, Emax preserved; **irreversible** = Emax lowered until the target is **resynthesized**.

segments.label: Definition
segments.value: reduction of an agonist's effect. It can occur **at the same receptor** (competitive or irreversible), **downstream** of the receptor (functional), **on the ligand** itself (chemical) or on its **pharmacokinetics**.

segments.label: How it works
segments.value: **competitive** (reversible, orthosteric site, weak bonds): the agonist curve shifts **right in parallel**, **Emax unchanged** → **surmountable** by increasing the agonist; the shift depends on the antagonist's concentration and affinity. **Irreversible/non-competitive** (covalent or allosteric binding): **↓ Emax** not recoverable; the effect ends only when the target is **resynthesized**.

segments.label: Clinical example
segments.value: competitive: **propranolol vs isoproterenol**, naloxone vs morphine, atropine vs acetylcholine. Irreversible: **phenoxybenzamine** (alkylates α receptors → phaeochromocytoma, started **before** the β-blocker), **clopidogrel/prasugrel** (P2Y12), **aspirin** (acetylates COX-1: **anucleate platelets** cannot resynthesize it → effect for **7–10 days**), **PPIs** (H⁺/K⁺ pump).

segments.label: Functional and chemical antagonism
segments.value: **functional**: an agonist at **another receptor** produces the opposite effect → **adrenaline in anaphylaxis** (β2 → ↑ cAMP → bronchodilation; α1 → vasoconstriction) against histamine and leukotrienes. **Chemical**: direct neutralization of the ligand → **infliximab/adalimumab** (TNF-α), bevacizumab (VEGF), protamine (heparin), **anti-digoxin Fab**.

segments.label: Exam trap
segments.value: **ibuprofen before aspirin**: by reversibly occupying platelet COX-1 it can prevent acetylation → **↓ antiplatelet effect** of aspirin. In anaphylaxis **IM adrenaline** comes **first**: antihistamines and corticosteroids are slow add-ons.

segments.label: Connections
segments.value: → aspirin (A5); P2Y12 (B12); PPIs (A11); α-blockers (B10); anti-TNF (A9); histamine (A6).

entries.name: Adaptations to repeated dosing: tolerance, tachyphylaxis, down/up-regulation, sensitization
entries.nameShort: Adaptations to repeated dosing: tolerance, tachyphylaxis, down/up-regulation, sensitization
entries.memo: Chronic agonist → **fewer receptors** (tolerance); chronic antagonist → **more receptors**: never stop a **β-blocker** abruptly.

segments.label: Definition
segments.value: **tolerance** = ↓ response to the same dose after repeated administration (days–weeks) → higher doses needed; often **partial** (only some effects). **Tachyphylaxis** = **rapid** tolerance (minutes–hours). **Sensitization** = ↑ response with repeated exposure. **Drug resistance** = complete loss of efficacy (antimicrobials, anticancer drugs).

segments.label: How it works
segments.value: pharmacodynamic mechanisms: target **desensitization** (phosphorylation by **GRKs** and binding of **β-arrestins** → uncoupling and internalization), **down-regulation** (↓ receptor number), mediator depletion, homeostatic counter-regulation. Pharmacokinetic: **enzyme induction** (↑ clearance). With chronic antagonists: **up-regulation/supersensitivity**.

segments.label: Clinical example
segments.value: **tachyphylaxis**: **ephedrine** and **tyramine** (indirect sympathomimetics) deplete the releasable noradrenaline pool; **nitrates** (→ nightly nitrate-free interval). **Down-regulation**: regular **β2-agonists** (↓ duration of bronchodilation; inhaled corticosteroids limit it). **Up-regulation**: **β-blockers** (abrupt withdrawal → tachycardia, angina, MI → **taper over 1–2 weeks**), clonidine (rebound hypertension).

segments.label: Why it matters
segments.value: **opioids**: **dissociated** tolerance — rapid to sedation, nausea, euphoria and (partly) analgesia; little to **constipation** and **miosis**; respiratory depression remains the lethal risk with rapid escalation, co-administered sedatives or after **loss of tolerance** (abstinence). **Sensitization**: psychostimulants (motor effects, craving), epileptic kindling, central sensitization in neuropathic pain.

segments.label: Exam trap
segments.value: **desensitization** (less responsive target, fast) ≠ **down-regulation** (fewer targets, slow); **tachyphylaxis** differs from tolerance by **time**. Tolerance can be **pharmacokinetic** (less drug at the receptor: induction) or **pharmacodynamic**.

segments.label: Connections
segments.value: → β2-agonists (A8); β-blockers and clonidine (B10); nitrates (B12b); opioids (B8); benzodiazepines (B1).

entries.name: Pharmacodynamic interactions: additivity, synergism, antagonism and cumulative effects
entries.nameShort: Pharmacodynamic interactions: additivity, synergism, antagonism and cumulative effects
entries.memo: **1+1 = 2** additivity, **1+1 = 3** synergism: useful when intended (lower doses), lethal when accidental (**benzodiazepines + alcohol/opioids**).

segments.label: Definition
segments.value: **additivity**: the combined effect = the **sum** of the effects («1 + 1 = 2»); **synergism (supra-additivity)**: effect **greater** than the sum («1 + 1 = 3»); **sub-additivity/antagonism**: effect **smaller**. Shown with an **isobologram** (line of additivity between the two drugs' EC50s).

segments.label: Why it matters
segments.value: used **intentionally**, additivity and synergism allow **lower doses** of each drug and therefore fewer dose-dependent adverse effects: **ACE inhibitor + thiazide** (also in fixed combinations), **β-lactam + aminoglycoside**.

segments.label: Clinical example
segments.value: **dangerous** synergisms: **benzodiazepines + alcohol** and **benzodiazepines + opioids** (respiratory depression, 2016 FDA warning); **nitrates + PDE5 inhibitors** (sildenafil: both ↑ cGMP → **severe hypotension**). Antagonism: **NSAIDs + ACE inhibitors/diuretics** (↓ renal prostaglandins → ↓ antihypertensive effect; with a diuretic, «triple whammy» → **acute kidney injury**).

segments.label: Cumulative toxicity
segments.value: ACE inhibitors/ARBs + **K⁺-sparing diuretics** (spironolactone, amiloride) ± trimethoprim or NSAIDs → **hyperkalaemia** (monitor K⁺ and creatinine, especially in renal failure, diabetes, the elderly); several **QT**-prolonging drugs → torsades de pointes.

segments.label: Exam trap
segments.value: synergism **does not require the same target**: drugs often converge on the same **physiological outcome** (respiratory centre, vascular tone). And an interaction may be **pharmacokinetic** (CYP, P-gp) rather than pharmacodynamic: say which in the exam.

segments.label: Connections
segments.value: → benzodiazepines (B1); opioids (B8); ACE inhibitors (B11); nitrates (B12b); aminoglycosides (Antibiotici-3); K⁺-sparing diuretics (B11b).

entries.name: Voltage-gated Na⁺ channels: three functional states and use-dependent block
entries.nameShort: Voltage-gated Na⁺ channels: three functional states and use-dependent block
entries.memo: Na⁺-channel blockers bind the channel **while it works**: they hit cells firing **too much** and spare the rest.

segments.label: Definition
segments.value: **α** subunit (~260 kDa) with **4 homologous domains (I–IV)**, each of **6** transmembrane **segments**: **S4** (positive residues) = **voltage sensor**; the **P loop** between S5 and S6 forms the **selectivity filter** (**tetrodotoxin** site); the intracellular **III–IV** loop is the fast **inactivation gate**.

segments.label: How it works
segments.value: **3 states**: **closed** (resting, activatable) → **open** (a few ms, Na⁺ influx, depolarization) → **inactivated** (non-conducting and **not re-activatable** → refractoriness) → back to closed on repolarization. **Local anaesthetics, class I antiarrhythmics and antiepileptics** reach their site when the channel is **open** and bind/stabilize the **inactivated** state.

segments.label: Why it matters
segments.value: **use-dependent block** (frequency- and voltage-dependent): the more a cell fires or is depolarized, the more channels are open/inactivated and the more drug binds → an **epileptic focus**, a **tachyarrhythmia**, a firing **nociceptive fibre** are blocked; normally firing tissues are spared = **functional**, not anatomical, selectivity.

segments.label: Clinical example
segments.value: class **IB** (lidocaine, mexiletine): **fast** dissociation → acts on **ischaemic/depolarized** tissue and at high rates; **IC** (flecainide, propafenone): **slow** dissociation → block even at normal rates (proarrhythmia in structurally diseased hearts); **IA** (quinidine, procainamide): intermediate + K⁺ block (↑ QT). Antiepileptics: phenytoin, carbamazepine, lamotrigine, lacosamide. Isoforms: **Nav1.1–1.3** (CNS), **Nav1.5** (heart, relatively tetrodotoxin-resistant), Nav1.7/1.8 (nociceptors).

segments.label: Exam trap
segments.value: selectivity is for the channel **state**, not the organ: after **overdose** or **intravascular injection** local anaesthetics also block CNS and heart → **seizures**, arrhythmias, arrest (bupivacaine is the most cardiotoxic).

segments.label: Connections
segments.value: → local anaesthetics (B2); class I antiarrhythmics (B13); antiepileptics (B9).

entries.name: Voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels (L, T, N, P/Q) and calcium channel blockers
entries.memo: **DHPs** → vessels, **verapamil** → heart, **diltiazem** in between; all act only on **L** channels. Absence seizures run through **T** channels.

segments.label: Definition
segments.value: pore-forming **α1** subunit (4 domains × 6 segments, S4 sensor) + accessory **α2δ** (disulfide-linked), **β** (intracellular) ± γ subunits. **High-voltage-activated (HVA)**: **L** (heart, smooth and skeletal muscle, endocrine cells), **N** (presynaptic terminals → transmitter release), **P/Q** (cerebellum, presynaptic), R. **Low-voltage-activated (LVA)**: **T** («transient»: SA node, **thalamus**).

segments.label: How it works
segments.value: **only L channels** are calcium-channel-blocker targets, with 3 allosterically coupled sites on α1: **dihydropyridines** (nifedipine, amlodipine…: domain III–IV segments; prefer the **inactivated** state at less negative potentials → **vascular smooth muscle**), **verapamil** (phenylalkylamine, IVS6, intracellular access, **use-dependent** block → SA/AV node), **diltiazem** (benzothiazepine, intermediate profile).

segments.label: Clinical example
segments.value: thalamic **T** channels → thalamocortical oscillations of **absence seizures** → **ethosuximide** (also valproate, zonisamide). **Gabapentin/pregabalin** do not act on α1: they bind **α2δ-1** → ↓ release of excitatory transmitters (neuropathic pain, focal epilepsy, generalized anxiety). **N** channels: ziconotide (intractable pain, intrathecal).

segments.label: Why it matters
segments.value: **verapamil or diltiazem + β-blocker** → bradycardia, AV block, heart failure. **Immediate-release DHPs** (nifedipine) → **reflex tachycardia** and possible **angina**; **ankle oedema** from precapillary vasodilation, which **does not respond to diuretics**.

segments.label: Exam trap
segments.value: in **skeletal muscle** the L channel (α1S) works as a **sensor** mechanically coupled to **RyR1**: contraction does not depend on extracellular Ca²⁺ → calcium channel blockers do not cause muscle weakness. Endocrine cells need only small Ca²⁺ entry → negligible effect on secretion.

segments.label: Connections
segments.value: → calcium channel blockers (B11); class IV antiarrhythmics (B13); antiepileptics (B9); Ca²⁺ homeostasis (G7); drug-induced angina (G7).

entries.name: K⁺ channels: voltage-gated (long QT), GIRK and K-ATP
entries.memo: Opening K⁺ channels **switches the cell off**, blocking them lengthens the action potential: drug-induced **long QT** is almost always **hERG**.

segments.label: Definition
segments.value: the most heterogeneous channel group; best classified by **function**: **voltage-gated** (repolarization), **Ca²⁺-activated**, **G-protein-coupled (GIRK)**, **ATP-sensitive (K-ATP)**. Opening them drives the potential towards **E_K** → hyperpolarization, ↓ excitability; blocking them **prolongs the action potential**.

segments.label: How it works
segments.value: **heart**: IKr (**hERG**/Kv11.1 channel) and IKs repolarize; **class III antiarrhythmics** (amiodarone, sotalol, dofetilide, ibutilide) block them → ↑ action potential duration and refractoriness → **↑ QT**. **GIRK**: opened by the **βγ** dimer of Gi/Go (vagal **M2** in SA/AV node, **A1** adenosine, **μ/δ** opioid, **α2**, GABA-B). **K-ATP** (Kir6.2 + **SUR**): ATP closes it → depolarization.

segments.label: Clinical example
segments.value: **β-cell**: glucose → ↑ ATP → K-ATP closure → depolarization → Ca²⁺ channels → **insulin**; **sulfonylureas and glinides** close the channel by binding **SUR1**; **diazoxide** opens it (insulinoma). **Minoxidil, nicorandil** open **SUR2B** → vasodilation. Neurons: **retigabine** opened KCNQ channels (antiepileptic, withdrawn for blue pigmentation). **Methylxanthines** block A1 receptors (excitatory effect).

segments.label: Why it matters
segments.value: **drug-induced long QT** = usually **off-target hERG block**, a channel with a cavity that binds many molecules: macrolides, fluoroquinolones, haloperidol and other antipsychotics, methadone, ondansetron, high-dose citalopram, tricyclics; antihistamines such as **terfenadine and astemizole** withdrawn. Risk ↑ with **hypokalaemia**, hypomagnesaemia, bradycardia, female sex, congenital long QT, metabolic inhibitors, combinations → **torsades de pointes**.

segments.label: Exam trap
segments.value: not all IKr blockers are equally dangerous: **amiodarone** prolongs QT markedly but rarely causes torsades (it also blocks Na⁺ and Ca²⁺); **verapamil** blocks IKr without torsades. Risk depends on the **multichannel** profile and the patient's conditions.

segments.label: Connections
segments.value: → class III antiarrhythmics (B13); sulfonylureas and glinides (A10); K-ATP channel openers (B12b); second-generation antihistamines (A6); antipsychotics (B5).

entries.name: P-type ATPases: Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase and digitalis, H⁺/K⁺-ATPase and proton pump inhibitors
entries.nameShort: P-type ATPases: Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase and digitalis, H⁺/K⁺-ATPase and proton pump inhibitors
entries.memo: Digoxin blocks the **Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase** → less Ca²⁺ exit via **NCX** → stronger heart; but with **low K⁺** it turns toxic.

segments.label: Definition
segments.value: pumps that use ATP to move ions **against their gradient** and **autophosphorylate on an aspartate** during the cycle (**E1 ⇄ E2** conformations): **Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase**, gastric **H⁺/K⁺-ATPase**, **Ca²⁺-ATPases** (SERCA, PMCA).

segments.label: How it works
segments.value: **Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase**: **3 Na⁺ out / 2 K⁺ in** per ATP → **electrogenic**; maintains the gradients that drive all secondary transporters. **α** subunit (catalytic: α1 ubiquitous and renal, **α2** muscle and heart, α3 neurons) + β; expression ↑ by aldosterone.

segments.label: Clinical example
segments.value: **digoxin**: binds the pump in the **phosphorylated E2** conformation from outside, **competing with K⁺** → ↑ intracellular Na⁺ → the **NCX** exchanger (3 Na⁺/1 Ca²⁺) extrudes less Ca²⁺ → more Ca²⁺ in the SR → **positive inotropy**; **vagal** effect → ↓ AV conduction (rate control in atrial fibrillation). **PPIs**: prodrugs activated in the acidic canaliculus → **covalent** binding to H⁺/K⁺-ATPase → **irreversible** inhibition (effect outlasting the 1–2 h plasma t½).

segments.label: Formula / key numbers
segments.value: digoxin = **narrow therapeutic index**: efficacy at concentrations **≤1 ng/mL**; toxicity ↑ with **hypokalaemia** (less competing K⁺ and an already depressed pump), hypomagnesaemia, hypercalcaemia, **renal failure**, old age, interactions (**amiodarone, verapamil, quinidine**). Signs: nausea and vomiting, **xanthopsia**, confusion, ectopy, **bidirectional ventricular tachycardia**, AV block. Antidote: **anti-digoxin Fab fragments**.

segments.label: Exam trap
segments.value: loop or thiazide diuretics + digoxin → **hypokalaemia** → digitalis toxicity even at «normal» levels. Conversely, severe acute poisoning comes with **hyperkalaemia** (pump blocked throughout the body).

segments.label: Connections
segments.value: → digitalis (B11b); PPIs (A11); diuretics (B11b); Ca²⁺ homeostasis (G7).

entries.name: Transporters as drug targets: renal epithelial (diuretics) and neurotransmitter transporters
entries.nameShort: Transporters as drug targets: renal epithelial
entries.memo: Diuretics block whoever reabsorbs **Na⁺** in the nephron; antidepressants and drugs of abuse act on whoever **takes back** neurotransmitters.

segments.label: Definition
segments.value: proteins that move solutes using the **Na⁺ gradient** built by the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase (secondary active transport) or the **H⁺** gradient (vesicular transporters). They are targets of **diuretics**, **antidepressants**, **antiepileptics** and **drugs of abuse**.

segments.label: How it works
segments.value: **kidney**: **NKCC2** (thick ascending limb, ~25% of filtered Na⁺) → **loop diuretics**; **NCC** (distal tubule) → **thiazides**; **ENaC** (collecting duct) → **amiloride, triamterene**; mineralocorticoid receptor → **spironolactone, eplerenone**; **SGLT2** → gliflozins. More Na⁺ reaching the collecting duct (loop, thiazides) = more K⁺ secreted → **hypokalaemia**.

segments.label: Clinical example
segments.value: **SLC6** (Na⁺/Cl⁻-dependent): **SERT** (SSRIs), **NET** (atomoxetine, tricyclics, SNRIs), **DAT** (bupropion; cocaine), **GAT-1** (**tiagabine** → ↑ synaptic GABA). **Vesicular** (H⁺ antiport): **VMAT2** (reserpine irreversibly → monoamine depletion; **tetrabenazine** in Huntington's chorea). Glial **EAATs** (EAAT1/2) take up glutamate and limit excitotoxicity; in **ischaemia** (↓ ATP, dissipated gradients) they can run **in reverse** and release it.

segments.label: Why it matters
segments.value: **reuptake** recycles the transmitter, **terminates** the signal and protects it from degradation: blocking it ↑ and prolongs transmission → therapeutic effect (antidepressants) or abuse (cocaine).

segments.label: Exam trap
segments.value: **cocaine** = **blocks** the transporter; **amphetamine** = a **substrate** that enters, empties vesicles (VMAT2) and **reverses** DAT/NET → impulse-independent release. Same target, different mechanism and toxicity.

segments.label: Connections
segments.value: → diuretics (B11b); SGLT2 inhibitors (A10); antidepressants (B3); tiagabine (B9); Huntington's disease and adjunct drugs (B6).

entries.name: The four receptor superfamilies: structure, signalling and response times
entries.nameShort: The four receptor superfamilies: structure, signalling and response times
entries.memo: Channels in **milliseconds**, GPCRs in **seconds**, enzyme-linked receptors in **minutes–hours**, nuclear receptors in **hours–days**.

segments.label: Definition
segments.value: **receptor** = macromolecule that recognizes an endogenous ligand (neurotransmitter, hormone, mediator) — and drugs that mimic or block it — and **transduces** the signal by changing cell function: via **ion fluxes**, **second messengers** (cAMP, cGMP, Ca²⁺, IP3/DAG) or **gene transcription**.

segments.label: Formula / key numbers
segments.value: **1) Ionotropic** (ligand-gated channels): **milliseconds** — pentamers (nAChR, GABA-A, glycine, 5-HT3) or tetramers (AMPA, NMDA, kainate). **2) Metabotropic/GPCRs** (7 transmembrane segments, a single chain): **seconds** — the largest family of drug targets. **3) Intrinsic enzyme activity**: **tyrosine kinase** receptors (insulin, EGF, VEGF, PDGF: dimerization + autophosphorylation → SH2/PTB-domain proteins → MAPK, PI3K-Akt) and membrane **guanylyl cyclase** (ANP/BNP → cGMP): **minutes–hours**. **4) Intracellular/nuclear** (**lipophilic** ligands): **hours–days**.

segments.label: Clinical example
segments.value: skeletal muscle contraction (nAChR, ms) · heart rate modulation (β1/M2, seconds) · growth and proliferation (receptor tyrosine kinases) · anti-inflammatory effect of glucocorticoids (GR, hours). Drugs: **imatinib, gefitinib** (tyrosine kinase inhibitors), **trastuzumab** (HER2), **cetuximab** (EGFR).

segments.label: Exam trap
segments.value: there are two **different** classifications: by **signalling mechanism** (the 4 superfamilies) and by **structure** (the «nicotinic superfamily» groups receptors with different ligands but the same architecture). The «times» refer to the **cellular response**, not binding; glucocorticoids also have rapid **non-genomic** effects.

segments.label: Connections
segments.value: → pentameric ligand-gated channels (G6); G proteins (G6); nuclear receptors (G6); targeted therapies (B14).

entries.name: Pentameric ligand-gated channel superfamily (nicotinic, GABA-A, glycine, 5-HT3) and tubocurarine
entries.memo: Five subunits, **M2** lining the pore: one template for nicotinic, GABA-A, glycine and 5-HT3 receptors. Charged **tubocurarine** stays peripheral.

segments.label: Definition
segments.value: ligand-gated channels made of **5 subunits**; each has a long **extracellular N-terminus** with a **disulfide**-closed loop («cys-loop»), **4 transmembrane segments (M1–M4)** — **M2** lines the pore — and an extracellular C-terminus. The ligand binds at **subunit interfaces** (2 agonist sites).

segments.label: How it works
segments.value: **nAChR** (Na⁺/K⁺ ± Ca²⁺ cations → excitatory): **muscle** type (α1)₂β1δγ in the fetus, with ε replacing γ in adults; **neuronal** α4β2 (nicotine, varenicline) and homomeric **α7**, highly **Ca²⁺**-permeable. **GABA-A** and **glycine** (Cl⁻ → inhibitory; glycine mainly spinal cord and brainstem, **strychnine** antagonist → convulsions). **5-HT3**: the only **ionotropic** serotonin receptor (area postrema, vagal afferents) → **«-setron»** antiemetics (ondansetron).

segments.label: Clinical example
segments.value: **tubocurarine** (active principle of curare): **competitive antagonist** of the muscle nAChR → flaccid paralysis (**non-depolarizing** neuromuscular blocker; today rocuronium, vecuronium, (cis)atracurium), reversed by anticholinesterases. It is a **quaternary ammonium**: permanent charge → crosses neither the **BBB** nor the gut mucosa → acts only peripherally.

segments.label: Why it matters
segments.value: phosphorylation of the muscle nAChR (PKA, PKC) modulates opening and **desensitization**; prolonged agonist exposure drives the channel into a **desensitized** state: the basis of succinylcholine block and of neuromuscular block by high-dose nicotine.

segments.label: Exam trap
segments.value: «tubocurarine for parkinsonian tremor?» → **no**: it does not enter the CNS; antiparkinsonian anticholinergics are **lipophilic central antimuscarinics** (biperiden, trihexyphenidyl).

segments.label: Connections
segments.value: → 5-HT3 antiemetics (A7); neuromuscular blockers in anaesthesia (B2); benzodiazepines and GABA-A (B1, G4); nicotine and addiction (G7); antiparkinsonian drugs (B6).

entries.name: Ionotropic glutamate receptors: AMPA and NMDA (Mg²⁺ block, LTP, excitotoxicity)
entries.nameShort: Ionotropic glutamate receptors: AMPA and NMDA
entries.memo: **NMDA** opens only with **glutamate + glycine + depolarization** (to expel Mg²⁺): a coincidence detector and the **Ca²⁺** gate.

segments.label: Definition
segments.value: **glutamate** is the main **excitatory** CNS transmitter; ionotropic **AMPA**, **NMDA**, **kainate** receptors (tetramers: the **M2 segment re-enters** the membrane without crossing it) and metabotropic **mGlu** receptors (group I → Gq; groups II–III → Gi/Go).

segments.label: How it works
segments.value: **AMPA** (GluA1–4): fast transmission, mainly Na⁺; with the (pore-edited) **GluA2** subunit it is **Ca²⁺-impermeable**, without GluA2 it becomes **Ca²⁺-permeable** (substrate of neurodegeneration and drug-induced plasticity). **NMDA** (GluN1 + GluN2): needs **glutamate** (GluN2) + **glycine/D-serine** co-agonist (GluN1) + **depolarization** that expels **Mg²⁺** from the pore → «**coincidence detector**»; high **Ca²⁺** permeability.

segments.label: Clinical example
segments.value: Ca²⁺ entering via NMDA → CaMKII, **nNOS** (NO as retrograde messenger) → **LTP/LTD** (hippocampus: learning and memory). **Excitotoxicity** (ischaemia, hypoglycaemia, trauma): massive release and reduced reuptake of glutamate → Ca²⁺ overload → **calpains**, ROS and peroxynitrite, mitochondrial damage → neuronal death.

segments.label: Drugs
segments.value: **memantine** (**low-affinity, use-dependent** NMDA antagonist → moderate–severe Alzheimer's), **ketamine** (channel block → dissociative anaesthesia; esketamine rapid antidepressant), phencyclidine; **perampanel** (non-competitive AMPA antagonist, antiepileptic); riluzole (↓ glutamate release, ALS).

segments.label: Exam trap
segments.value: **Mg²⁺** is not a competitive glutamate antagonist: it is a **voltage-dependent pore block** → NMDA conducts only if the membrane is already depolarized (by AMPA). That is why a use-dependent blocker such as memantine spares physiological transmission.

segments.label: Connections
segments.value: → memantine (B7); ketamine (B2); antiepileptics (B9); Ca²⁺ homeostasis (G7).

entries.name: G protein–coupled receptors (GPCRs): Gs, Gi, Gq and the muscarinic, adrenergic and dopaminergic systems
entries.memo: **Gs** ↑ cAMP, **Gi** ↓ cAMP and opens K⁺, **Gq** ↑ IP3/Ca²⁺: muscarinic **odd = Gq, even = Gi**; **α2** is the only Gi adrenoceptor.

segments.label: Definition
segments.value: **GPCR** = a single chain with **7 transmembrane segments** (extracellular N-terminus; third intracellular loop and C-terminus coupled to the G protein). **Heterotrimeric αβγ** G protein: at rest α binds **GDP**; the activated receptor exchanges GDP for **GTP** → α-GTP and **βγ** separate and regulate effectors; α's **GTPase** activity ends the signal. Large **amplification**.

segments.label: How it works
segments.value: **Gs** → ↑ adenylyl cyclase → ↑ **cAMP** → PKA (β1, β2, β3, D1/D5, H2, 5-HT4, V2). **Gi/Go** → ↓ cAMP; **βγ** opens K⁺ channels (GIRK) and closes N-type Ca²⁺ channels (α2, M2/M4, D2–D4, μ/δ/κ, GABA-B, CB1, 5-HT1A). **Gq** → **PLCβ** → **IP3** (Ca²⁺ from ER) + **DAG** (PKC) (α1, M1/M3/M5, H1, AT1, 5-HT2).

segments.label: Clinical example
segments.value: **muscarinic**: **odd Gq, even Gi** → cardiac M2 (vagus: ↓ rate and AV conduction), M3 glands and smooth muscle, M1 CNS and stomach. **Adrenergic**: α1 Gq (vasoconstriction, mydriasis, prostate), **α2 Gi** (presynaptic autoreceptors → ↓ noradrenaline release; central **clonidine** → ↓ sympathetic outflow), β Gs. **Dopaminergic**: D1-like (D1, D5) Gs; **D2-like** (D2, D3, D4) Gi → antipsychotic target.

segments.label: Phosphodiesterases and cholera toxin
segments.value: **phosphodiesterases (PDEs)** switch off cAMP and cGMP: theophylline (non-selective, also an adenosine antagonist), **milrinone** (PDE3, inotrope), **sildenafil/tadalafil** (PDE5), roflumilast (PDE4). **Cholera toxin** locks Gs in the active state → high enterocyte cAMP → secretory diarrhoea.

segments.label: Exam trap
segments.value: **α2** is the only **Gi** adrenoceptor: an adrenergic agonist (clonidine) **lowers** blood pressure by acting centrally; abrupt withdrawal causes **rebound**. Nitrates + PDE5 inhibitors → both ↑ cGMP → **severe hypotension**.

segments.label: Connections
segments.value: → antimuscarinics (A8, A11); clonidine and α1-blockers (B10); β2-agonists and theophylline (A8); antipsychotics (B5); histamine (A6).

entries.name: Intracellular (nuclear) receptors: genomic and non-genomic mechanisms
entries.memo: **Lipophilic** ligand → receptor in cytosol or nucleus → **DNA**: slow effect (hours) that **outlasts** the drug.

segments.label: Definition
segments.value: transcription factors activated by **lipophilic** ligands that cross the membrane: **cytosolic** at rest (bound to **HSP90**: glucocorticoids, mineralocorticoids, androgens, progestins) or already **nuclear** (oestrogens, thyroid hormones, vitamin D, retinoic acid, PPARs, PXR/CAR).

segments.label: How it works
segments.value: domains: N-terminal **transactivation**, **DBD** with two **zinc fingers** (cysteines coordinating Zn²⁺) that recognize specific DNA sequences (**HREs**, e.g. GRE), hinge region, **LBD** (ligand pocket). Sequence: binding → release from HSP → **dimerization** → nucleus → HRE → recruitment of **co-activators/co-repressors** → ↑/↓ transcription (e.g. glucocorticoids: inhibition of **NF-κB/AP-1**).

segments.label: Formula / key numbers
segments.value: **latency** of hours (cellular effects) and days (full clinical effect); the effect **outlasts** the drug's presence in the circulation (biological duration > plasma t½, typical of corticosteroids).

segments.label: Clinical example
segments.value: drugs: **glucocorticoids**, **SERMs** (tamoxifen, raloxifene), antiandrogens (bicalutamide), **levothyroxine**, **calcitriol**, **ATRA** (acute promyelocytic leukaemia), **glitazones** (PPARγ), **fibrates** (PPARα); **rifampicin** acts on **PXR** → enzyme induction.

segments.label: Exam trap
segments.value: because of their latency, glucocorticoids are **not** first-line in acute bronchospasm or anaphylaxis (**adrenaline** and β2-agonists first) — even though rapid **non-genomic** effects (minutes), mediated at the membrane, exist.

segments.label: Connections
segments.value: → glucocorticoids (A4); SERMs (A12); enzyme inducers (G2); glitazones (A10).

entries.name: Classical neurotransmitters and neuropeptides; autoreceptors and retrograde signalling (endocannabinoids, NO)
entries.nameShort: Classical neurotransmitters and neuropeptides; autoreceptors and retrograde signalling
entries.memo: A classical transmitter **transmits** (fast, local, taken back up); a neuropeptide **modulates** (slow, at a distance, degraded by peptidases).

segments.label: Definition
segments.value: **classical neurotransmitter** (acetylcholine, glutamate, GABA, glycine, monoamines): made in the **terminal**, concentrated in **small synaptic vesicles**, released by **Ca²⁺-dependent exocytosis** at active zones (N and P/Q channels) even with a single action potential; **fast, local** action; terminated by **reuptake** (DAT, NET, SERT, GAT, EAAT) or **enzymes** (acetylcholinesterase).

segments.label: How it works
segments.value: **neuropeptides** (endogenous opioids, CRH, NPY, substance P, CGRP, oxytocin): made in the **soma** as precursors (e.g. **POMC**), stored in **large dense-core vesicles**, released **outside active zones** only with **repetitive or high-frequency firing**; they also act at a distance (**volume transmission**) as **modulators**; inactivated by **peptidases** (no reuptake).

segments.label: Clinical example
segments.value: **co-transmission**: one neuron releases a classical transmitter plus a peptide or ATP (noradrenaline + **NPY** + ATP; acetylcholine + **VIP**) with different release thresholds. Presynaptic **auto- and heteroreceptors** give negative feedback: **α2** (noradrenaline), somatodendritic **5-HT1A** and terminal 5-HT1B/1D, D2, GABA-B, M2 → **mirtazapine** blocks α2 → ↑ release of noradrenaline and serotonin.

segments.label: Why it matters
segments.value: **retrograde signalling**: **endocannabinoids** (anandamide, **2-AG**) are made «on demand» in the postsynaptic neuron and activate presynaptic **CB1** (Gi/Go, abundant in the brain) → ↓ release; **NO** (a gas made by Ca²⁺-activated neuronal NO synthase) diffuses to the terminal and activates **soluble guanylyl cyclase** → cGMP.

segments.label: Exam trap
segments.value: neuropeptides are **not** taken back up like monoamines and need intense stimulation: hence their slow, diffuse, «behavioural» effect. **CRH** is both a **hormone** (pituitary axis) and a **neurotransmitter** (amygdala, locus coeruleus).

segments.label: Connections
segments.value: → endogenous opioids and cannabinoids (B8); mirtazapine (B3); NMDA and NO (G6); HPA axis and CRH (G7).

entries.name: Catecholamines: biosynthesis, degradation (MAO, COMT) and marker metabolites
entries.memo: **Tyrosine hydroxylase** controls synthesis; **MAO-A** clears NA, 5-HT and **tyramine**, **MAO-B** dopamine.

segments.label: Definition
