segments.value: **tyrosine → L-DOPA** (**tyrosine hydroxylase**, TH: **rate-limiting enzyme**, cofactor tetrahydrobiopterin) **→ dopamine** (aromatic L-amino acid decarboxylase, AADC or DOPA decarboxylase) **→ noradrenaline** (dopamine **β-hydroxylase**, inside vesicles) **→ adrenaline** (**PNMT**, mainly in the adrenal medulla). **VMAT2** loads vesicles; **NET** takes back most (~87%) of released noradrenaline.

segments.label: How it works
segments.value: **MAO** (mitochondrial): **MAO-A** → noradrenaline, serotonin and dietary **tyramine** (gut, liver); **MAO-B** → dopamine (CNS, platelets). **COMT**: acts only on **catechols** (so not on serotonin).

segments.label: Marker metabolites
segments.value: **noradrenaline/adrenaline → VMA** (urine: **phaeochromocytoma**) and MHPG (central noradrenaline turnover); **dopamine → DOPAC and HVA** (HVA is the main metabolite, an index of dopamine turnover); **serotonin → 5-HIAA** (MAO only; urine: **carcinoid syndrome**).

segments.label: Clinical example
segments.value: **levodopa + carbidopa/benserazide** (**peripheral** AADC inhibitors that do not cross the BBB); **entacapone, opicapone, tolcapone** (COMT); **selegiline, rasagiline, safinamide** (MAO-B); irreversible non-selective **MAOIs** + **tyramine**-rich foods → **hypertensive crisis** («cheese effect»), lower risk with **moclobemide** (reversible MAO-A). **MPTP → MPP⁺** (via MAO-B) → taken up by **DAT** → inhibits mitochondrial complex I → death of nigral dopaminergic neurons → parkinsonism and experimental model.

segments.label: Exam trap
segments.value: a **raised metabolite** does not always mean more synthesis: it may reflect more release and breakdown or more exposure from **reuptake block** (cocaine) → read it together with the transmitter and the clinical picture. Inhibiting AADC barely lowers tissue noradrenaline stores: the rate-limiting step is **TH**.

segments.label: Connections
segments.value: → levodopa, COMT and MAO-B inhibitors (B6); MAOIs (B3); α-methyldopa (B10); phaeochromocytoma and phenoxybenzamine (G4).

entries.name: Drug-induced (iatrogenic) angina: mechanisms and culprit drugs
entries.memo: Mechanism first (reflex tachycardia, coronary spasm, sympathetic rebound), then the drugs: that is how to answer in the exam.

segments.label: Definition
segments.value: onset or worsening of **myocardial ischaemia** caused by drugs, especially in patients with **coronary artery disease**. A classic exam question: answer **mechanism first**, then drug classes.

segments.label: How it works
segments.value: myocardial **O₂ demand** depends mainly on **heart rate**, contractility and afterload; tachycardia also shortens **diastole**, when the coronaries fill → with fixed stenoses demand exceeds supply. Four mechanisms: **(A)** vasodilation/hypotension → **reflex tachycardia** (baroreflex); **(B)** direct **coronary vasoconstriction**; **(C)** ↑ **sympathetic tone** (direct or rebound); **(D)** drug cardiotoxicity or hypertension.

segments.label: Clinical example
segments.value: **(A)** **immediate-release nifedipine**, hydralazine, minoxidil, first dose of **α1-blockers**; **dipyridamole** dilates healthy arterioles and «steals» flow from ischaemic areas. **(B)** **triptans** and **ergots** (contraindicated in ischaemic heart disease), **cocaine**, amphetamines, α-agonist decongestants, **5-fluorouracil/capecitabine** (vasospasm). **(C)** **abrupt β-blocker withdrawal** (or clonidine), sympathomimetics (dobutamine, adrenaline), levodopa, MAOIs + tyramine, excess **levothyroxine**. **(D)** anthracyclines, anti-VEGF drugs, coxibs.

segments.label: Why it matters
segments.value: in a hypertensive coronary patient prefer **slow-onset dihydropyridines** (amlodipine) or combination with a **β-blocker**; **taper** β-blockers; avoid triptans; long-acting nitrates need a **nitrate-free interval** (tolerance) but must not be stopped abruptly.

segments.label: Exam trap
segments.value: do not list drugs at random: starting from the **baroreflex** and **coronary flow physiology** shows you understand why opposite drugs (a vasodilator and a vasoconstrictor) can cause the same symptom.

segments.label: Connections
segments.value: → calcium channel blockers (B11, G5); triptans and ergots (A7); β-blockers (B10); nitrates (B12b); 5-FU and anticancer drugs (B14); up-regulation (G4).

entries.name: Intracellular Ca²⁺ homeostasis: channels, stores (IP3R, RyR), pumps (SERCA, PMCA) and NCX
entries.memo: Ca²⁺ enters through **channels**, leaves the **stores** (IP3R, RyR), is cleared by **SERCA, PMCA, NCX**: when control fails, the cell dies.

segments.label: Definition
segments.value: free Ca²⁺ is **~1–1.2 mM** outside and **~100 nM** in the cytosol (~10,000-fold gradient); most cellular Ca²⁺ is **bound** (calmodulin, calsequestrin) or in **stores** (endo/sarcoplasmic reticulum, mitochondria). Free Ca²⁺ is the **signal**: contraction, secretion, transmitter exocytosis, transcription, apoptosis.

segments.label: How it works
segments.value: **entry**: voltage-gated channels (L, N, P/Q, R, T), ligand-gated channels (NMDA, GluA2-lacking AMPA, α7 nAChR), receptor-operated channels and **SOCE/CRAC** (the ER sensor **STIM1** detects depletion and opens plasma-membrane **ORAI1**). **Release from stores**: **IP3R** (via Gq → PLC → IP3) and **RyR** (Ca²⁺-induced Ca²⁺ release: RyR2 in heart; RyR1 in skeletal muscle, coupled to the L channel).

segments.label: Ca²⁺ removal
segments.value: **SERCA** (refills the reticulum; regulated by phospholamban), **PMCA** (high-affinity extrusion, activated by calmodulin), **NCX** (3 Na⁺ in / 1 Ca²⁺ out: high capacity, depends on the Na⁺ gradient), **mitochondria** (buffer during overload).

segments.label: Clinical example
segments.value: **digitalis**: ↓ Na⁺ gradient → ↓ NCX extrusion → ↑ SR Ca²⁺ → inotropy. **Dantrolene**: inhibits **RyR1** → malignant hyperthermia (**RYR1/CACNA1S** variants → susceptibility to volatile anaesthetics and succinylcholine). **Ciclosporin and tacrolimus** inhibit **calcineurin** (Ca²⁺/calmodulin-dependent phosphatase). Glucocorticoids induce **annexin-1** (binds Ca²⁺ and phospholipids) → ↓ phospholipase A2.

segments.label: Exam trap
segments.value: when Ca²⁺ rises uncontrolled (ischaemia, excitotoxicity) **calpains**, phospholipases and caspases are activated and mitochondria are damaged: injury becomes irreversible. In **skeletal muscle** contraction does not need extracellular Ca²⁺ (mechanical L channel–RyR1 coupling); in the **heart** it does.

segments.label: Connections
segments.value: → Ca²⁺ channels (G5); digitalis (B11b, G5); glutamate and excitotoxicity (G6); anaesthetics (B2); glucocorticoids (A4).

entries.name: Nicotine, the α4β2 receptor and the addiction circuit (varenicline)
entries.nameShort: Nicotine, the α4β2 receptor and the addiction circuit
entries.memo: Nicotine → **α4β2** in the **VTA** → dopamine in the **nucleus accumbens**: **varenicline** (a partial agonist) eases craving and blunts the reward.

segments.label: Definition
segments.value: at the concentrations reached by smoking, nicotine acts mainly on the high-affinity **neuronal α4β2 nAChR**, expressed on **dopaminergic neurons of the ventral tegmental area (VTA)**, rather than on the muscle receptor.

segments.label: How it works
segments.value: nicotine → α4β2 → depolarization of VTA neurons → ↑ **dopamine** in the **nucleus accumbens** (ventral striatum: encodes **value/reinforcement**) → the **dorsal striatum** learns the associated **action** (the act of smoking) and turns it into a **habit**. Repeated exposure **desensitizes** receptors → tolerance and need for higher doses.

segments.label: Clinical example
segments.value: **varenicline**: **α4β2 partial agonist** → stimulates enough to ease **craving** and withdrawal and, by occupying the receptor, **reduces the reinforcement** of smoked nicotine. Other options: **bupropion** (DAT/NET), nicotine **replacement therapy** (transdermal patches, gum).

segments.label: Why it matters
segments.value: **craving** is tied to associative **memory** and **stress** (CRH in the amygdala): it is the real treatment target. According to the lecture, individual vulnerability depends largely on the **endogenous opioid system** (the same one that sets pain threshold), not only on nicotinic receptor numbers.

segments.label: Exam trap
segments.value: a **partial** agonist has a **dual role**: without nicotine it acts as an agonist (less withdrawal), with nicotine as an **antagonist** (less reward). Do not confuse it with a pure antagonist.

segments.label: Connections
segments.value: → partial agonists (G4); pentameric ligand-gated channels (G6); bupropion (B3); HPA axis and CRH (G7).

entries.name: HPA axis, CRH and circadian rhythms in drug therapy (chronopharmacology)
entries.nameShort: HPA axis, CRH and circadian rhythms in drug therapy
entries.memo: Cortisol and noradrenaline **peak in the morning**: corticosteroids **in the morning**, first **α1-blocker** dose **at bedtime**.

segments.label: Definition
segments.value: **CRH** (paraventricular nucleus) acts as a **hormone** (portal blood → **ACTH** from POMC → **cortisol** from the zona fasciculata, with negative feedback) and as an extrahypothalamic **neurotransmitter** (amygdala, locus coeruleus): anxiety, stress response, negative affect of **withdrawal**, **relapse**. **Metabolic** effects (hyperglycaemia, catabolism) belong to **cortisol**, not CRH.

segments.label: How it works
segments.value: cortisol acts on **MR** (high affinity, occupied even at basal levels) and **GR** (low affinity, recruited by stress or therapy) → **inverted-U** curve for learning and memory (hippocampus): moderate levels favour synaptic potentiation, excessive or chronic levels impair it (traumatic memories, post-traumatic stress disorder).

segments.label: Circadian rhythm
segments.value: cortisol **peaks on waking** (early morning) and is lowest in the evening/night; at the same time a **noradrenergic surge** (locus coeruleus) ↑ blood pressure and heart rate → **morning peak** of infarctions, strokes and arrhythmias.

segments.label: Clinical example
segments.value: **glucocorticoids** as a single **morning** dose (mimic the rhythm, ↓ axis suppression; possibly alternate-day regimens); antihypertensives with **24-h coverage** including the early morning; **α1-blockers** (prazosin, doxazosin): «**first-dose effect**» (orthostatic hypotension, syncope) → start with a **low dose at bedtime**, then titrate slowly.

segments.label: Exam trap
segments.value: «all antihypertensives should be taken in the evening» → not proven: a large pragmatic trial (TIME, 2022) found no difference in events between morning and evening dosing; **24-h coverage** is what matters. The bedtime rule applies to the **first dose** of α1-blockers.

segments.label: Connections
segments.value: → glucocorticoids (A4); α1-blockers (B10); anxiety (B1); nicotine and addiction (G7).
